records.sourceFile: Media's effect on athletes' mental health.pdf

paper.citation: Ng T, Sanders H, Merrill S, Faustin M. Media's effect on athletes' mental health. Clin Sports Med. 2023.
paper.abstract: The authors review how traditional and social media affect athletes' mental health. They cover media obligations, coverage of female and minoritized athletes, social media use, and the pressure of media attention on elite athletes.
paper.tldr: Media attention can add real stress for elite athletes, female athletes receive less and more appearance-focused coverage, and athletes from minoritized backgrounds can face stereotyped coverage and online abuse. Research on athletes' mental health and social media is still limited.
paper.methods: Narrative clinical review with no search method reported. The authors describe media obligations by competition level, summarise studies of media coverage and social media, and draw on high-profile cases and small qualitative studies of athletes.
paper.findings: Professional and Olympic athletes are usually required by written agreements to speak to the media, and collegiate athletes often need administrative approval. The authors report that female athletes receive less media coverage than male athletes, and that coverage often focuses on appearance. Qualitative studies describe media attention as a source of stress for elite athletes, including a study of four male and six female athletes who had each won at least two gold medals. The authors also cite a systematic review of 13 studies linking social media use to depression, anxiety and distress in the general population, and state that no major studies address athletes' mental health and social media directly.
paper.limitations: The review gives no search or appraisal method, and the authors note that little research addresses athletes' mental health and social media directly. Much of the cited evidence comes from general-population or small qualitative studies, and several examples are high-profile news cases.
paper.practicalImplications: Sports medicine staff can check whether athletes understand their media obligations and have media training, particularly collegiate athletes who face NIL-related pressure to build an online presence. Periods of heavy media attention, such as major events, title wins and difficult losses, are reasonable times to check in, since the cited qualitative studies link them with stress. The review does not offer screening tools or thresholds.
paper.athleteDev: Include media preparation and a check on media pressure in athlete support planning, especially around major events and for athletes building a social media profile. Treat coverage of female and minoritized athletes as a context factor rather than a predictable effect on any individual.
paper.rtp: This review covers media effects on the mental health of competitive athletes. It does not address concussion, injury recovery or return-to-play decisions and should not be used to guide return to sport after injury.

records.sourceFile: Neurodiversity in elite sport - A systematic scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: Hoare E, Reyes J, Olive L, Willmott C, Steer E, Berk M, et al. Neurodiversity in elite sport: a systematic scoping review. BMJ Open Sport and Exercise Medicine. 2023;9:e001575.
paper.abstract: A systematic scoping review of 23 studies on neurodivergence (mainly ADHD, also autism and specific learning disorders) in elite sport, searched to May 2023. The studies were 10 observational studies, 4 reviews, 6 commentary or position statements and 3 qualitative studies. The authors found very limited research, mostly on ADHD in US college athletes, and no intervention studies.
paper.tldr: Research on neurodivergent athletes in elite sport is very limited and mostly concerns ADHD, concussion and medication rules. The authors conclude that neurodiversity-inclusive practice is not yet evidence-based in elite sport.
paper.methods: Systematic scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, with six databases searched through the EBSCOhost platform to 12 May 2023 and reference lists checked. Title and abstract screening was done by one author, a second reviewer checked 10% of articles, and a third reviewer resolved discrepancies.
paper.findings: Of 23 included studies, 10 were observational, mostly in US college athletes, and most focused on ADHD as a risk factor for concussion and its management. Other work covered ADHD prevalence, stimulant medication under anti-doping rules, and lived experience from three qualitative studies, one of which examined autism in elite French athletes. The authors found no studies of interventions or environmental practices for neurodivergent athletes.
paper.limitations: The authors note small sample sizes and self-report measures of neurodevelopmental differences, which are open to individual bias. Grey literature was not searched, and the authors acknowledge that relevant studies may have been missed. The definition of athlete populations varied across studies.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors state that coaches and performance staff need education on the sensory, emotional and cognitive needs of neurodivergent athletes, and that healthcare staff would likely benefit as well. Staff should note that evidence-based inclusive practices are limited in elite sport.
paper.athleteDev: Performance and coaching staff may need to understand neurodivergent athletes, since learning and skill development are central to performance. The review found no studies of performance outcomes or coaching approaches for neurodivergent athletes, and any performance advantage linked to ADHD or autism is unconfirmed.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport or rehabilitation. It reports that ADHD may affect baseline concussion screening performance and that findings on prolonged concussion recovery remain mixed. It provides no return-to-play criteria and should not be used to set return-to-play decisions for neurodivergent athletes.
